subject: Chemistry
title: Nuclear Transmutation: Alchemy Achieved
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Nuclear Transmutation: Alchemy Achieved.

hook.text: In 1919, Rutherford turned nitrogen into oxygen by bombarding it with alpha particles. Transmutation was real.

buildup.text: He fired helium nuclei at nitrogen gas. Some nitrogen atoms absorbed a proton and became oxygen.

discovery.text: This was the first artificial nuclear transmutation—changing one element into another, just as alchemists dreamed.

twist.text: In 1980, scientists transmuted bismuth into gold using a particle accelerator. But it cost far more than the gold was worth.

climax.text: Alchemy's dream came true through nuclear physics—not chemical reactions. The alchemists had the right dream, wrong method.

punchline.text: Smash atoms, change elements. The alchemists' dream needed nuclear physics.

quiz.question: Who first achieved artificial transmutation of one element into another?
options: Ernest Rutherford, turning nitrogen into oxygen in 1919
Marie Curie, while studying radium in 1898
Albert Einstein, through his mass-energy equation

details.summary: In 1919, Ernest Rutherford achieved the first artificial nuclear transmutation by bombarding nitrogen atoms with alpha particles to produce oxygen, fulfilling alchemy's ancient dream through nuclear physics rather than chemistry..
details.whyItMatters: Nuclear transmutation proved alchemists were conceptually correct that elements could be transformed. The technology spawned nuclear energy, medical radioisotopes, and the creation of elements beyond uranium.
takeaways: Rutherford first transmuted nitrogen into oxygen using alpha particles in 1919
Nuclear reactions change atomic number, achieving alchemical transmutation
Creating gold from mercury is possible but costs far more than the gold's value

faq.question: Can we actually create gold from other elements today?
faq.answer: Yes. In 1980, scientists at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory bombarded bismuth with high-energy particles in a particle accelerator and produced a few atoms of gold. However, the energy cost was astronomical, making each atom far more expensive than natural gold..

faq.question: How does nuclear transmutation differ from what alchemists attempted?
faq.answer: Alchemists tried to transform elements through chemical reactions, which only rearrange electrons and bonds without changing atomic nuclei..
